title: A Lopsided War: 83,000 Soldiers and Police Powering Indonesia’s Violent Agenda in Papua
description: Soldiers and police have increasingly encroached on Papuans’ daily lives, not only to maintain security but also to advance a development agenda built on violence. For more than half a century, armed conflict has raged in Papua. Throughout this period, the Indonesian government has conducted military operations, deploying tens of thousands of soldiers and police […]
content: Soldiers and police have increasingly encroached on Papuans’ daily lives, not only to maintain security but also to advance a development agenda built on violence. For more than half a century, armed conflict has raged in Papua. Throughout this period, the Indonesian government has conducted military operations, deploying tens of thousands of soldiers and police to a lopsided war it still cannot win. To understand the current situation, we must look back to 1969, when the western part of New Guinea officially became Indonesian territory following the Act of Free Choice, known locally as Pepera. Many Papuans, however, refer to it as “the act of no choice” because Indonesian military and intelligence forces marred the process with intimidation and manipulation. The New Order military regime, which had recently come to power, persuaded the United Nations and Western governments that the Papua issue should be resolved through “deliberation toward consensus”. The regime claimed that most Papuans were uneducated and therefore unfit to make such a decision. Following this colonial and racist logic, Indonesian officials and UN representatives selected 1,026 Papuans they deemed eligible to take part. Soon after, they all reached a “consensus” to join Indonesia. Rebellion emerged shortly after Pepera, culminating in the proclamation of the Republic of West Papua by Seth Jafeth Roemkorem and Jacob Prai on July 1, 1971. The Indonesian military responded with overwhelming force, swiftly crushing what was then a sporadic resistance movement. Since then, Indonesia’s military presence in Papua has intensified to confront the pro-independence movement, including the various factions and wings of the Free Papua Organization (OPM). One such group is the West Papua National Liberation Army (TPNPB), OPM’s armed wing. Over time, soldiers and police have increasingly encroached on Papuans’ daily lives, not only to maintain security but also to advance a development agenda built on violence. No wonder Papua now has Indonesia’s heaviest concentration of security forces, both military and police. Our research shows that at least 83,177 soldiers and police officers are currently deployed across six provinces in Papua. Of that total, 56,517 are from the Indonesian Armed Forces (TNI) and 26,660 from the National Police (Polri). These figures cover only “organic” forces, meaning personnel assigned to Papua-based units, rather than temporary reinforcements deployed from elsewhere. Given the uncertainty around the number of TNI troops deployed, we used multiple methods to estimate personnel across the Army (AD), Navy (AL), and Air Force (AU). For the Air Force, we compiled details on its units from a range of documents and cross-checked our findings through interviews. We also analyzed photographs, including flag-ceremony images, to estimate personnel in smaller units such as radar units (Satrad) and air bases (Lanud). For the Navy, we reviewed documents related to Fleet Command (Koarmada) III, headquartered in Sorong, Southwest Papua, which is responsible for maritime defense in eastern Indonesia. We calculated personnel for Marine Force (Pasmar) 3, which includes an Infantry Brigade (Brigif), Marine Base Defense Battalions (Yonmarhanlan) in three areas, Combat Support Regiments (Menbanpur), and several small detachments. For the Army, we examined internal documents, cross-checked our findings in the field, and reviewed media coverage and social media posts from relevant units. Police figures in Papua, meanwhile, were easier to compile from official documents and news reports, as the police have been relatively transparent about their numbers. We could not, however, determine the number of intelligence personnel, including officers from the State Intelligence Agency (BIN), who are coordinated through its regional offices (BINDA). This report also excludes troops deployed from outside Papua under the Operational Command Authority (BKO) mechanism. These personnel typically serve on annual rotations. We plan to publish a separate article examining the various BKO task forces operating in Papua. Even using conservative estimates, and without counting BKO task forces, the numbers we present in this report remain substantial. According to police data, 24 separatist networks operate in Papua with 1,438 members. They have only 361 firearms, and otherwise rely on traditional weapons such as spears and machetes. With 83,177 soldiers and police present, the number of organic forces in Papua is 58 times larger than the membership of these separatist groups. Statistics Indonesia (BPS) data show the combined population of six provinces in Papua reached about 5.8 million in 2025. With 56,517 TNI personnel and 26,660 Polri personnel, there is one soldier for every 103 Papuan residents and one police officer for every 219 residents. Nationally, the ratios are dramatically different. In 2024, BPS recorded Indonesia’s population at 281.6 million, with 404,500 TNI personnel and 464,248 Polri personnel. That translates to about one soldier for every 696 residents and one police officer for every 607 residents, a stark contrast to the figures in Papua. Nor does it stop there. The government has designated Papua, Jakarta, and Aceh as Indonesia’s defense “centers of gravity”. In these three regions, the TNI plans to bolster defenses and expand the use of radar. As a result, Papua is all but certain to see an even larger military buildup. Force Deployment Air Force The Commando Battalion 468/Sarotama of the Indonesian Air Force’s Rapid Action Forces Corps (Kopasgat) conducts a refresher parachute jump exercise, with the drop zone on the runway of Frans Kaisiepo Airport in Biak Numfor, Papua, on Jan. 22, 2025. (Indonesian Air Force) The Air Force assigns Papua and the Maluku Islands to Air Operations Command (Koopsud) III, which was recently renamed Air Force Regional Command (Kodau) III and is headquartered in Biak Numfor. Kodau III oversees two Type A Air Bases (Lanud) in Biak Numfor and Jayapura, two Type B Lanud in Merauke and Timika, and one Type C Lanud in Wamena. President Prabowo Subianto’s administration aims to develop additional Lanud, including in Nabire. The headquarters in Biak Numfor also hosts Air Squadron 27, which operates CN-235 aircraft for intelligence collection, and Air Wing 9, which is responsible for technical support and the operation of military aircraft and their crews. Commando Battalion 468/Sarotama of the Rapid Action Forces Corps (Kopasgat) is also based there. The Air Force maintains detachments in Sorong, Nabire, South Manokwari, and Merauke, and operates Radar Units (Satrad) in Biak Numfor, Timika, Merauke, Jayapura, Sorong, and Kaimana. Kodau III’s headquarters in Biak Numfor hosts the largest concentration of Air Force personnel. Based on our calculations, at least 2,500 personnel are stationed there. Personnel numbers at other locations depend on base type and whether a Satrad is present. Type A Lanud typically have about 1,200 personnel, while Type B and Type C bases have 355 and 167 personnel, respectively. Each Satrad operates with around 40 personnel, including radar technicians and security forces. Taken together, our conservative estimate puts the number of Air Force personnel in Papua at a minimum of 4,817. This figure could rise as additional military units are established under Prabowo’s administration. Navy Frogmen from Fleet Command (Koarmada) III conduct a long-distance open-water swim exercise in the waters off Sorong, West Papua, on Aug. 30, 2021. (Koarmada III) The Navy maintains Fleet Command (Koarmada) III, which oversees maritime defense in eastern Indonesia. Its headquarters is in Sorong. Prabowo Subianto’s administration is reorganizing the Navy to give it a structure similar to the Army’s. As a result, each Koarmada now has a Naval Regional Command (Kodaeral), an arrangement akin to the Army’s Regional Military Commands (Kodam). Put simply, Kodaeral is a maritime version of a Kodam. Under this structure, Kodaeral oversees Naval Military Resort Commands (Korem Laut), which in turn manage several Navy Main Bases (Lantamal) and Navy Bases (Lanal). At the lowest level are Maritime Potential Development NCOs (Babinpotmar), the Navy’s equivalent of the Army’s Village Development NCOs (Babinsa). Koarmada III now controls three Kodaeral: Kodaeral X in Jayapura, Kodaeral XI in Merauke, and Kodaeral XIV in Sorong. Under them are several Lanal and smaller units, including Navy Posts (Posal) and Marine Posts (Posmar). We estimated Navy personnel across eight regions in Papua, including staff at Kodaeral and Lanal headquarters and at combat units such as Infantry Brigade (Brigif) 3/Marine and Marine Base Defense Battalions (Yonmarhanlan). Sorong, home to Koarmada III and Kodaeral XIV headquarters, hosts at least 5,440 personnel. Jayapura and Merauke, hosting Kodaeral X and XI respectively, station 2,690 and 2,215 personnel. Overall, there are at least 12,910 Navy personnel in Papua. Once again, this is a highly conservative estimate, and the figure is likely to grow as new Lanal and Posal are built under the government’s expansion plans. Army Army personnel represent the largest contingent, totaling 38,790 soldiers, or 68.6% of all organic TNI personnel in Papua. We have broken down the data by territorial units and combat forces. Territorially, the Army divides Papua into three Military Regional Commands (Kodam): Kodam XVII/Cenderawasih in Jayapura, Kodam XVIII/Kasuari in Manokwari, and Kodam XXIV/Mandala Trikora in Merauke. In 2026, the government plans to establish two new Kodam, one in Nabire, Central Papua, and the other in Sorong, Southwest Papua. Each Kodam oversees varying numbers of Military Resort Commands (Korem). Kodam XVII/Cenderawasih has three, Kodam XVIII/Kasuari has two, and Kodam XXIV/Mandala Trikora has one. Each Korem oversees Military District Commands (Kodim). Papua has 29 Kodim, short of the ideal, as each regency and city is expected to have one. Papua has 40 regencies and two cities. Each Kodim oversees Military Subdistrict Commands (Koramil). The number of Koramil corresponds to the number of subdistricts. As of 2025, Papua has 306 subdistricts. Meanwhile, each village is meant to have a Village Development NCO (Babinsa). Papua has 4,443 villages. Interviews for this report suggest that, as of 2025, only about 40% of those villages had a Babinsa. We have analyzed territorial Army personnel across Papua. This figure excludes the two Kodam that officials plan to establish in 2026. The Army maintains “organic” combat forces, meaning personnel assigned to Papua-based units. Some battalions fall under Kodam and Korem, while others are under the Army Strategic Reserve Command (Kostrad) or the Army Special Forces Command (Kopassus). Kodam XVII/Cenderawasih operates across three provinces: Papua, Highland Papua, and Central Papua. The military is restructuring this command. Maj. Gen. Amrin Ibrahim, commander of Regional Military Command (Kodam) XVII/Cenderawasih, visits a military post in Jayawijaya, Highland Papua, on Nov. 7, 2025. (Kodam XVII/Cenderawasih) The military plans to establish a Kodam for Central Papua in 2026. Korem 173/PVB, formerly based in Biak Numfor, has moved to Nabire in Central Papua to serve as the nucleus of the new command. It will relocate Infantry Brigade (Brigif) 20/IJK from Timika to Nabire to support the Central Papua Kodam. Brigif 20/IJK comprises two Infantry Battalions (Yonif): Yonif Raider 754/ENK in Timika and Yonif Raider 755/Yalet in Merauke. This brigade operates under Infantry Division 3/Kostrad. Jayapura hosts Yonif 751/VJS, Combat Engineer Detachment (Denzipur) 10/KYD, and Denzipur 12/OHH. The city also houses a Kodam Training Regiment (Rindam), which provides education and training. Moreover, the military has reinforced Kodam XVII/Cenderawasih with units designated for “territorial development” (“teritorial pembangunan” in Indonesian, or TP). These units are intended to strengthen defense while also supporting development and agriculture. For example, Brigif TP 80/Kurare and Brigif TP 82/WKB each command five Territorial Development Infantry Battalions (Yonif TP). Yonif TP 815/WGT is based in Keerom under Korem 172/PWY. Another Yonif TP is reported to operate in Paniai, although its unit designation remains unclear—the Defense Ministry listed it in its 2025 planning documents. A typical Army battalion has 700 personnel, divided into three or four rifle companies and a headquarters company. TP battalions are similar in size, but instead of rifle companies they include agriculture, animal husbandry, fisheries, and health companies. In total, two Brigif TP and 12 Yonif TP serve under Kodam XVII/Cenderawasih. In addition, Joint Defense Area Command (Kogabwilhan) III is headquartered in Mimika, home to PT Freeport Indonesia’s mining operations. It serves a combat coordination role. Mimika is also set to become the base for Kopassus Group 6, with three battalions to be redeployed from Jakarta. Kogabwilhan III’s tactical command post is seen in Mimika, Central Papua. The unit reports directly to the TNI Commander and coordinates combat forces in Papua. (Google satellite imagery) Overall, Kodam XVII/Cenderawasih hosts 19 combat battalions and three combat detachments. A typical battalion has 700 personnel, while a detachment has 168. A Kogabwilhan headquarters is typically staffed by 542 personnel. Under our moderate estimate, there are a total of 14,346 combat personnel in the Kodam XVII/Cenderawasih area. Meanwhile, Kodam XVIII/Kasuari was formed in 2016 after being split off from Kodam XVII/Cenderawasih. Headquartered in Manokwari, it covers West Papua and Southwest Papua. Kodam XVIII/Kasuari soldiers practice martial arts at the Kodam headquarters field in Manokwari, West Papua, on Oct. 10, 2024. (Kodam XVIII/Kasuari) This Kodam fields Yonif 761/KA and Combat Engineer Battalion (Yon Zipur) 20/PPA, as well as Brigif 26/GP with three Yonif units: Yonif 762/VYS, Yonif 763/SBA, and Yonif 764/LB. Korem 181/PVT in Sorong has one TP battalion, Yonif TP 863/BB, while Korem 182/JO in Fakfak has Yonif TP 808/MM. Five additional Yonif TP operate under Brigif TP 84/UA in South Manokwari. Overall, Kodam XVIII/Kasuari has 12 combat battalions. Seven are Yonif TP units formed in 2025, bringing the estimated number of combat personnel under this command to about 8,400. While the figure is smaller than that for Kodam XVII/Cenderawasih, the Kodam XVIII/Kasuari area also includes the Navy Fleet Command (Koarmada) III headquarters. In 2026, the military plans to establish a new Kodam in Southwest Papua by splitting it off from Kodam XVIII/Kasuari. Brig. Gen. Eventius Teddy Danarto, the chief of staff of Kodam XXIV/Mandala Trikora, is welcomed at the Kodam’s headquarters in Merauke, South Papua, on Sept. 22, 2025. (Kodam XXIV/Mandala Trikora) Kodam XXIV/Mandala Trikora is the newest military command in Papua, created by upgrading Korem 174/ATW in Merauke. President Prabowo Subianto announced its establishment on Oct. 10, 2025. Kodam XXIV/Mandala Trikora covers all of South Papua. It has three Kodim, in Merauke, Boven Digoel, and Mappi. The military plans to establish a fourth in Asmat. This Kodam includes Yonif 757/GV and Denzipur 11/MA. Its largest combat unit, Brigif TP 83/Bugodi, commands six Yonif TP. The military also plans to establish Yonif TP 861 in Wanam Village, the site of the Prabowo administration’s food and energy estate. In early October 2024, near the end of his term as defense minister, Prabowo established five Vulnerable Area Support Infantry Battalions (Yonif PDR) in Papua, including two in South Papua. The units were created to support and oversee government programs in the region. Soldiers harvest 4 hectares of rice fields in Wanam Village, Merauke, South Papua, on May 16, 2025. (Indonesia’s Agriculture Ministry) In early December 2024, after Prabowo became president, the military redesignated all Yonif PDR as Yonif TP. Soldiers from these TP battalions are now clearing land for the Merauke food and energy estate, planned to cover 2.6 million hectares. Of that total, 1 million hectares is slated for sugarcane plantations and bioethanol factories. As a result, Papuan customary land and forests continue to shrink. Overall, Kodam XXIV/Mandala Trikora has eight Yonif battalions and one Denzipur. By our moderate estimate, this Kodam has 5,768 combat personnel. We sought confirmation from Maj. Gen. Freddy Ardianzah, a TNI spokesperson. We asked about the number of “organic” troops stationed in Papua, the personnel figures we identified, and the rationale for establishing new units in Papua. We sent these questions on Dec. 3, 2025, but had received no response by the time of publication. Police At present, Papua has two provincial police commands (Polda): Papua Regional Police and West Papua Regional Police. Although Papua was split into six provinces in 2022, four new Polda have yet to be established. Papua Regional Police now covers four provinces: Papua, South Papua, Central Papua, and Highland Papua. Meanwhile, West Papua Regional Police covers two: West Papua and Southwest Papua. According to a report by Jubi, a local media outlet in Jayapura, Papua Regional Police currently has 15,854 personnel. By the police’s own calculations, that figure falls well short of the staffing level they consider ideal, which is 28,848 personnel. Meanwhile, West Papua Regional Police has 8,343 personnel, even though its ideal staffing level is 15,392. Papua Regional Police, together with the Cartenz Peace Operation, a joint police and military task force, conducts an investigation in Puncak Jaya, Central Papua, on July 27, 2024, following unrest on July 16. (Indonesian National Police) The police also conduct security operations through the Mobile Brigade (Brimob). Each provincial police command typically fields one Brimob battalion. Brimob forces are essentially combat units, with specialized training in urban security and urban warfare. Brimob also has Gegana units that specialize in counterterrorism, bomb disposal, and crowd control. Papua Regional Police currently fields two Brimob battalions and one Gegana detachment, totaling 2,063 personnel. The police plan to add two more battalions: one in Wamena, Highland Papua, and one in Biak Numfor, Papua. Meanwhile, West Papua Regional Police inaugurated its Brimob unit in June 2025 with 400 personnel. A War with No Victor Given the scale and distribution of military and police personnel across Papua today, a host of questions arise. What is driving this massive military expansion, and to what end? Does Indonesia really need such a large force for so-called security and development? How much money is the government spending on it? And most importantly, with such a large security presence, why has Indonesia still been unable to resolve the separatism issue in Papua? We will try to answer these questions one by one in our reporting series on #PrabowosWarRegime in Papua, beginning with this article. A hint: Timor-Leste. In 1975, the New Order government created a conflict of its own by invading Timor-Leste, then known as East Timor. Indonesia’s occupation did not end until 1999, after the people of Timor-Leste held a referendum and voted to separate from Indonesia. Over more than 23 years in Timor-Leste, thousands of Indonesian soldiers were killed in combat. Tens of trillions of rupiah, or hundreds of trillions in today’s value, were spent to subdue the territory, rebuild it, and install a puppet government. A series of military operations was launched to crush resistance in Timor-Leste. An estimated 20% of the population died during the occupation, largely from hunger, illness, and other fallout from Indonesian military operations. Yet the Timorese resistance never died. Movement leaders who survived gunfire or arrest kept fighting, and went on to inspire a new generation. Indonesia never fully conquered Timor-Leste, despite its overwhelming superiority in training, weaponry, and other military capabilities. In the end, Indonesia gained nothing. Only loss and death. Made Supriatma is a Visiting Fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, and an Early Warning Fellow at the Simon-Skjodt Center for the Prevention of Genocide at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum. Fahri Salam is editor-in-chief of Project Multatuli. Johanes Hutabarat contributed to this article. Anne Parisianne translated the original Indonesian piece, and Viriya Singgih edited the English version. This is the first article in our #PrabowosWarRegime reporting series. The series exposes how Indonesia’s war machine is being deployed in Papua, fueling a climate of fear, killings, dehumanization, and waves of displacement that have forced indigenous Papuans to flee their own land.

author: Sonia Bhaskar
title: ‘Not Too Late to Regulate AI,’ Says Empire of AI’s Author Karen Hao
description: Author Karen Hao argues that while the cost of Silicon Valley-led AI expansion is being borne by the Global South, there are ways to reverse this narrative and build collaborative AI systems that benefit all. As the dependence on artificial intelligence increases and tech companies across the world invest heavily in data center facilities, award-winning […]
content: Author Karen Hao argues that while the cost of Silicon Valley-led AI expansion is being borne by the Global South, there are ways to reverse this narrative and build collaborative AI systems that benefit all. As the dependence on artificial intelligence increases and tech companies across the world invest heavily in data center facilities, award-winning reporter and author of Empire of AI, Karen Hao, argues this scale of development is “unnecessary”. She says that this narrative about building larger data centers has been solidified and sold to the public and policymakers. The expansion, which Hao refers to as “imperial expansion”, is happening at the cost of communities and resources which are scarce. While highlighting the widening Global North and Global South divide, she opines that the AI development should be a cross-border endeavor. In this conversation with Sonia Bhaskar, Hao also focuses on the role of governments to regulate AI and says that AI should lead to public benefit, rather than benefitting a few “that are running these Silicon Valley companies”. The interview has been edited for brevity. What have been some of the more alarming developments you’ve noticed recently in the AI industry? Sam Altman, just a few weeks ago, said that he envisions just for his company, OpenAI, building 250 gigawatts worth of data centers by 2033, which he estimates could cost 10 trillion dollars. 250 gigawatts. A reporter actually compared this to the entire amount of energy demand in India and so that would be an extraordinary increase in energy demand globally, and most of that would be powered by fossil fuels, because that is the energy available. I want to emphasize that this scale is actually technically unnecessary. Even if we didn’t have that scale, we would still have AI. And yet, they’re trying to build larger and larger data center facilities, supercomputer facilities, around the world, and have sold a narrative to the public and policymakers that this is required for getting more AI capabilities. The Global North and South divide seems to be widening with this kind of model of AI development. Are these countries geared up to even counter the threat coming their way? There are a lot of activists, organizations, and communities themselves that have taken big leadership roles in countering this kind of expansion, which I describe in my book as a form of imperial expansion. One of the anecdotes that I highlighted in my book was of these Chilean water activists that were very concerned about a proposed Google data center landing into their community. And it was a project that was sanctioned by the Chilean government, it was one that the Chilean govt in fact celebrated, because they considered it to be a mark of economic development for the country, of participating in this technological revolution, but what the community and the water activists saw on the ground was that it was taking their already scarce fresh water resources, and without their consent, they had not been notified of this project. They actually discovered it after someone tipped them off, that was not supposed to tip them off. They then pushed back aggressively on the proposal, so they started mobilizing, talking with every single one of the neighbors within that community, explaining to them in plain terms, what exactly having a data center within this community could mean for their ability to access fresh water, and they built up so much public support that they were able to pass a referendum to block the project before there was further investigation into the environmental impacts. And then they went even further and escalated to Google Mountain View, where Google Mountain View had to evaluate, make concessions to the community, and then they escalated to the Chilean government, which has now created this roundtable that brings together community residents and activists, as well as the tech companies, to discuss future data center projects in the country. So that kind of spirit, even when there aren’t government protections from imperial expansion projects, and even when the government is actually in cahoots with the companies to bring even more of these facilities in, we have seen remarkable mobilizing where the community steps up, and they take the leadership and are able to still gain significant concessions, and even block projects completely, when it’s not within their interest. How do you see the role of Asia in terms of the incoming data center investments and a source of cheap labor? Basically any time a chatbot or an AI system can do anything, it has to be taught by a human. And because chatbots are language technologies, these companies will look to contract cheap English-speaking workers. And because of the history of colonialism with the UK colonizing India, or the US colonizing places like the Philippines, those are places where there is a large base of English-speaking workers that can perform a task that these tech companies want them to do. In my book, I highlight this example of how OpenAI contracted an Indian firm to do content moderation on their models for image generation. So, these workers were looking through all of this really horrific AI-generated images to try and figure out which ones should be allowed or not allowed with OpenAI’s technologies. In the Philippines there’s also a huge base of data industry workers, not just chatbots, but they are doing things like labelling images or they’re trying to train self-driving cars. And all of these workers work in often extremely exploitative conditions. Because the workers are not actually told who they’re working for, they’re often unclear on who the boss even is. Like if there are problems they’re seeing, they don’t even know who to flag it too. And they’re also often paid very, very little amount of money, maybe a couple dollars a day, or a couple dollars an hour, depending on where they sit geographically, and how much these companies think they can get away with. So it has become more and more of a problem, as the industry has continued to grow and the labor demand has continued to grow. We see three models: the US (big tech, concentrated power/profit), China (state-backed incentives and narrative control), and the EU (cautious regulation, with talk of General Data Protection Regulation or GDPR relaxation). Where do you think the solution lies? What features of these models offer the most just and sustainable path for AI’s wide-reaching societal and economic impact? China’s case illustrates something that we have seen for a long time, which is that in resource constrained environments there’s actually much more innovative AI work being done. So in my own interactions with researchers around the world, some of the most exciting research is by African AI researchers, or Latin American researchers, or Chinese AI researchers, because they’re just not operating under the same circumstances, of having an extraordinary amount of money or computational resources. They’re developing models that aren’t just the same as American models in terms of capabilities, with just less resources, but they’re also looking at fundamentally different types of AI technologies that are centering the problem that they ultimately want to solve with AI. So, with African AI researchers that I’ve spoken to in the past, grid reliability is a huge issue, not just in Africa but actually around the world. And they’ve figured out how to create very small, specialized AI models to improve grid reliability such as simply predicting when a piece of grid equipment is going to fail before it fails so they can swap in newer equipment, upgrade it, and not have any kind of blackout, or downtime, for that grid. And these are things that the U.S. has really underinvested in because they’re just not pursuing this kind of thinking anymore. I sort of see it as they’ve become intellectually lazy because of a glut of capital and glut of resources. So, they’re not looking at how do we actually just solve these very practical problems that can improve the quality of life and human rights around the world. Before Silicon Valley really entered the scene with realizing that there was a significant amount of money to be made in the AI industry, AI research was largely a cross-border endeavor. It was understood that if everyone around the world works together to build AI, we will just end up with better systems that improve lives for everyone. And so that is where I see the solution. We rewind the narrative of zero-sum game, like all of these competing models, and who’s going to win and who’s going to lose. We rewind all of that back to the narrative that once reigned, which was that we actually have cross-border collaboration, and that the best ideas can come from anywhere in the world, and everyone can take advantage of them. Who should regulate AI, and what role should the government play? We failed to regulate social media, nowhere in the world have we successfully managed to do that. AI seems to be getting out of control and when we combine that with issues of mis and disinformation, deepfakes, privacy, security—what model of regulation can work? How can we learn from our mistakes in the past? So first, I think we need a broader understanding of what even constitutes AI regulation. I think a lot of people think that regulating AI simply means allowing anyone to build AI, however they want, and then deciding how to constrain the deployment of that technology into the world. But actually, we also need to consider how AI is developed in the first place. So the fact that these American companies have just been scraping whatever data they want, and hoovering up all of this intellectual property without any hindrance—that is a place where the government should be intervening. They should be interpreting copyright law to strengthen intellectual property protections. The U.S. should please have a federal data privacy law, so that there’s actual protections from people having their children’s photos caught up in training these systems, that ultimately then can be used to harm their kids. The data centers need to be regulated—that is also a form of AI regulation, where all governments should be thinking, within their own country’ context. What land would they actually allow these companies to build on? How much energy would they actually want these companies to be able to use for this type of technology? How much freshwater would they use? And there might be plenty of actually existing regulations that already apply, like environmental regulation, that were originally designed to check other industries and their pollution, that are actually extremely relevant for the AI industry as well. So the question when you say, who should regulate—the answer is everyone. Every government should be thinking about how to design regulations that help steer the trajectory of AI development so that ultimately leads to broad public benefit, rather than just benefits concentrated in the hands of the wealthy that are running these Silicon Valley companies. And that requires looking at the full AI development supply chain, and also the deployment scenarios, and there will need to be international coordination of course. So we need to use all of the regulatory instruments that are available to us, that we already have, to also contain the way that the AI industry is currently creating a lot of harm. It’s never too late to do that. Because these companies require up-to-date data in order to continue developing their models, they require up to date computer chips for training the next generation of their facilities. So we might have missed the boat for the things that already exist now, but that doesn’t mean that we cannot regulate that’s going to exist in the future. In order for the companies to continue keeping up with the innovative feel, they need to develop new things. It’s not like, suddenly, OpenAI can continue cashing in on a ChatGPT that was generations older. So all of the things that are going to come after, the many AI technologies that come after, it’s absolutely not too late for us to actually implement regulation. In fact, we have a lot of evidence now from the last three years of this technology being around, of how to actually design this effective regulation for all the technologies moving forward. There’s been talk of an AI bubble building up. What’s your estimate of where we’re headed over the next year and what are the bright spots you see in this landscape? There’s a huge bubble. I am very concerned that it’s going to burst in a way that is extremely harmful to the global economy and is going to leave a lot of people around the world devastated. But if there is a bubble pop, journalism is still essential. Community efforts, public education, and civil society work is still essential to figure out how do we rebuild after the bubble pops. There’s, been plenty of work done by people like Naomi Klein, who have shown that in crisis, in disaster situations, there are two ways we can come out of it: a) Authoritarian, fascists, corporate opportunists use that crisis to then make things worse: install more surveillance, to erode more human rights, to privatize everything, b) It becomes a place for the phoenix to rise from the ashes. We are able to build something fundamentally better by going back to what are the real core things that we want to protect as a society, that are crucial to human flourishing, and how do we rebuild even better, more resilient institutions, communities, organizations, around those core principles. All of the work we do now as public defenders, whether activists, advocates, or non-profit work, government work, journalism, all of that work is going to help determine which path we take. You have drawn parallels between AI empires and colonial extraction. Where do you see this empire going, and where do we go from here as a society? It did take a long time to unwind colonialism, but it happened. And it happened at a time when there wasn’t really a broad understanding of democracy. This global belief in fortifying human agency and human rights, and making sure that people have the freedom to choose how they self-govern and what kind of future they ultimately want to live in. So we’re in a much better place now, where we actually know those things, and people are willing to fight for them because they already have tasted that. So one thing that I see is like, the immune system response that’s been happening to these new empires has happened much, much faster than in the past, and we know for a fact that throughout history, empires have fallen, and this time it will be no different. Cameraperson: Hashim Hakeem Video Producer: Anoushka Dalmia Video Editor: Shivansh Srivastava This story was produced by Asian Dispatch and originally published on November 27, 2025. It has been republished by Project Multatuli with permission.

author: Iqbal Lubis
title: Bantaeng’s Dust Season: Living on the Front Lines of the Nickel Boom
description: Residents around the Bantaeng Industrial Park must live with thick dust and the constant roar of nickel smelters that are steadily damaging their health and the environment. The “national strategic project” the government promotes as a road to prosperity has instead become a source of seemingly endless hardship. Ambo One afternoon in October 2025, thick […]
content: Residents around the Bantaeng Industrial Park must live with thick dust and the constant roar of nickel smelters that are steadily damaging their health and the environment. The “national strategic project” the government promotes as a road to prosperity has instead become a source of seemingly endless hardship. Ambo Ambo Enre, 77, has witnessed every change that has come to Papanloe village in Pa’jukukang, Bantaeng. Since the Bantaeng Industrial Park began operating, he has never received any aid from the companies behind the “strategic” project. He lives in a dilapidated stilt house, coated in ever-present dust drifting in from the industrial site. (Project M/Iqbal Lubis) One afternoon in October 2025, thick black smoke billowed from the stack of a nickel smelter in Pa’jukukang district, Bantaeng, South Sulawesi. Carried by the wind, it crept beneath a gray sky, seeping into nearby neighborhoods and unsettling residents’ lives. For local residents, it’s an everyday sight. Under the government’s push for downstream nickel processing, foreign-backed companies have built smelters across Pa’jukukang. Much of the development is concentrated in a roughly 3,200-hectare area spanning six villages, designated as the Bantaeng Industrial Park (BIP). The transformation has upended daily life in surrounding communities. Take Ambo Enre. The 77-year-old resident of Papanloe village in Pa’jukukang lives in a stilt house wedged between two nickel smelter facilities that run day and night. “If the companies came and saw for themselves, maybe they would understand how we live under the smoke,” said Ambo. “When the wind blows this way, my eyes sting, my breathing gets shallow.” Two years ago, his wife moved to their child’s home just 10 meters away as her health deteriorated. “She was constantly coughing and struggling to breathe,” said Ambo. Ambo has lived in this house since 2005. From here, he has witnessed every change that has come to Pa’jukukang. Ambo Enre shows the dust accumulating in his living room. His stilt house in Papanloe village stands between two nickel smelter facilities operating day and night. His wife has moved to another home after developing a persistent cough and breathing difficulties. (Project M/Iqbal Lubis)Ambo Enre shows a thick layer of dust coating his feet. Each day, dust from two nickel smelter facilities drifts into his home, settling on the floor and in every corner. He must wash his feet repeatedly, but when he’s too exhausted, he sometimes goes to bed with them still dust-covered. (Project M/Iqbal Lubis)A wall decoration in Ambo Enre’s house, where dust coats nearly every corner, drifting in from two nickel smelters operating day and night. (Project M/Iqbal Lubis) In 2013, China’s Huadi Group, the main investor behind the BIP, began acquiring land for the project. According to the Balang Institute and the Mining Advocacy Network (Jatam), the process was rife with intimidation. PT Huadi Nickel-Alloy Indonesia, a part of Huadi Group, began building its smelter complex in Pa’jukukang in 2014. Yet the company only started preparing its environmental impact assessment (Amdal) in 2015. In early 2016, the government designated BIP a national strategic project (PSN), a status that eased approvals and strengthened state backing, including for permits and land acquisition. PT Huadi Nickel-Alloy Indonesia’s smelter was formally inaugurated in January 2019, after undergoing production trials in 2018. More smelters followed, including those built by PT Hengsheng New Energy Material Indonesia, PT Unity Nickel Alloy Indonesia, PT Dowstone Energy Material Indonesia, PT Huadi Wuzhou Nickel Industry, PT Yatai Huadi Alloy Indonesia, and PT Huadi Yatai Nickel Industry. Jatam’s investigation says these firms are all part of the Huadi Group. Since then, the once green and idyllic Papanloe village has slowly turned barren. Ambo and other residents once farmed small plots behind their homes, growing chili peppers, vegetables, and cassava. Now the soil is dry and hardened, blanketed in dust. “There’s no arable land left,” Ambo said. Ambo Enre mixes soil to mold bricks. To make ends meet, he now works as a brickmaker at a neighbor’s small home workshop. He remembers Papanloe as a green, quiet village, where families farmed small plots behind their houses, growing chili peppers, vegetables, and cassava. (Project M/Iqbal Lubis) Ambo’s stilt house is now dilapidated. The wooden frame is rotting, the walls are pocked with holes, and the corrugated metal roof has rusted and begun to leak. Still, he refuses to leave. “I want to stay here. This is my home,” he said, looking up at the tarpaulin ceiling, now brown and thick with dust. “I was born here, I grew up here, and when the time comes, I want to be buried here.” An aerial view of nickel smelters operated by PT Hengsheng New Energy Material Indonesia at the Bantaeng Industrial Park (BIP) in South Sulawesi. The complex borders residential homes in Papanloe village, where residents contend with dust pollution every day. (Project M/Iqbal Lubis) Raba Not far from Ambo Enre’s home, Raba Intang, 80, swept the floor of her child’s house. Her wrinkled hands gripped the broom as she moved it slowly back and forth, raising dust from the concrete floor, now stained a different color. “It’s good I don’t have to sweep 15 times a day anymore, since the factory behind this house hasn’t resumed operations,” Raba said in a thick Makassar accent. Since July 15, 2025, Huadi Group has suspended operations at some of its smelters in the Bantaeng Industrial Park (BIP), as prices for processed nickel products slumped amid a global oversupply. According to the Indonesian Nickel Miners Association (APNI), three Huadi Group companies have halted plant activities: PT Huadi Nickel-Alloy Indonesia, PT Huadi Wuzhou Nickel Industry, and PT Huadi Yatai Nickel Industry. As a result, more than 1,000 workers were furloughed. On Nov. 17, PT Huadi Nickel-Alloy Indonesia sent a letter to Bantaeng regency’s manpower and industry office, notifying officials that it would lay off 510 workers on Nov. 21, citing “losses” and “efficiency” as the reasons. The notice came without prior warning. The BIP chapter of the Mining and Energy Industry Workers Union (SBIPE) quickly learned of the news and staged a protest on Nov. 19. “The recent wave of layoffs has deepened our concerns about a pattern of repeated violations by the company: claiming losses without evidence, carrying out mass layoffs, and failing to meet its obligations to workers,” the SBIPE’s BIP chapter said. The precarious lives of the workers add to the growing list of hardships Bantaeng residents have faced since the industrial park arrived. Thick layers of dust coat the windowpanes of a resident’s home in Papanloe village, which is wedged between two nickel smelter complexes operated by PT Hengsheng New Energy Material Indonesia and PT Unity Nickel Alloy Indonesia. (Project M/Iqbal Lubis) According to Raba, when the factories were all running, dust drifted in constantly and settled in every corner of the house. “There was no break from cleaning, in the morning, at noon, or at night, right up until bedtime,” said Raba, who was wearing a brown house dress printed with “Luois Viutto” when she was interviewed. “If everything starts up again, the dust will return. We’ll be the first to suffer.” Raba Intang, 80, stands in front of the house she no longer lives in. She moved to her child’s home because she could no longer endure the deafening noise and the sulfur stench from nearby smelters. Even there, dust still drifts in, forcing her to sweep up to 15 times a day. (Project M/Iqbal Lubis) Before moving to her child’s place, Raba lived nearby in a stilt house. Her house is now in poor shape. The corrugated metal roof is riddled with holes, as if pelted with stones. The walls are blackened. The wooden pillars no longer stand straight and have begun to rot. “I can’t live there anymore,” she said. “At night, the noise from the factories cuts through the bedroom walls. Not to mention the smell.” After the move, the noise and stench eased. But Raba still struggles with her health. “Coughing is just part of life here,” Raba said. So far, neither the government nor the companies have taken concrete steps to address the mounting harms from large-scale nickel processing at the BIP. More trees are withering, the air is increasingly difficult to breathe, and residents’ living space continues to shrink. Nickel-processing waste from PT Huadi Nickel-Alloy Indonesia piled near homes in Mawang hamlet, Bantaeng, South Sulawesi. (Project M/Iqbal Lubis) Residents can only bear the burden in silence, watching as their farmland has been turned into an industrial estate and the whir of machinery has replaced the sounds of crickets and irrigation canals. “There’s no compensation. There’s no ‘dust money’ that was promised,” said Raba. That afternoon, the dust returned. Out on the yard, Raba was sweeping again, moving the broom back and forth in a Sisyphean routine, in a village reshaped by an industrial boom. Sulfa Students at Pa’jukukang State Junior High School (SMPN) 3 play kasti, a local bat-and-ball game, on the school field during P.E. Since PT Hengsheng New Energy Material Indonesia’s smelters began operating in 2023, the school has grappled with dust, stench, and the constant drone from the nearby plant during class hours. (Project M/Iqbal Lubis) Across the road from Borongloe village, also in Pa’jukukang, a narrow alley led me to a school blanketed in dust. The gates looked dull. The nameplate was almost illegible beneath a thick brown coating. This is Pa’jukukang State Junior High School (SMPN) 3. It’s located just under 200 meters from nickel smelters operated by PT Hengsheng New Energy Material Indonesia, which have been running since 2023. The library at Pa’jukukang State Junior High School (SMPN) 3 sits empty, with its shelves and furniture coated in dust from the nearby industrial park. Enrolment has fallen as parents send their children to larger towns and cities to escape the pollution. (Project M/Iqbal Lubis) That morning, the first lesson had just begun. On a field fringed with tall grass and banana trees, about a dozen students played kasti, a local bat-and-ball game, during P.E. The rubber ball flew. Students ran to catch it. A teacher stood at the edge of the field, jotting notes in a small notebook. Behind them, two smokestacks loomed, sending black smoke into the sky. Not a single student wore a mask. They were used to it, the teacher said, referring to the smoke, dust, and sulfur stench. “Throw the ball!” one student shouted. “Ruuun!” another yelled. Laughter rang out through the dust. Outside the field, three girls took a break: Resky, Latifa, and Sulfa. They were breathing heavily. Latifa coughed now and then. “Don’t take pictures of the factories. Take pictures of us,” Sulfa said with a smile. “People come here to take photos all the time, but the school is still dusty and it’s so noisy when we’re trying to study.” A corner of a classroom after it has been swept. Dust from PT Hengsheng New Energy Material Indonesia’s nickel smelters in Pa’jukukang district, Bantaeng, continues to drift into the rooms and is difficult to remove. (Project M/Iqbal Lubis) Inside a classroom with faded yellow walls, Tanti, not her real name, drew a chart on the whiteboard. She wore a mask. There were no educational posters or motivational quotes on the walls, only dust stains that seemed permanent. “Every time I go home, my shirt isn’t white anymore. It turns brown,” she said. The vents in every room are now covered with plastic to keep out the dust. But it barely helps. Every morning before classes begin, students and teachers must sweep away the dust that settles overnight from the smelters. “If the dust is especially heavy, we close the school,” said Ibrahim, the headmaster. The problem extends beyond the classrooms. The school laboratory, for instance, has been left unused, with its tables and walls blanketed in dust. “We can’t use this anymore,” a teacher said. Dust-filled classrooms have become the new normal at Pa’jukukang State Junior High School (SMPN) 3. With limited funding from the School Operational Assistance (BOS) program, the school cannot hire cleaning staff, leaving students and teachers to do the sweeping. But no matter how often they clean, the dust returns, along with the ceaseless drone and clang of nearby factories. (Project M/Iqbal Lubis) Covering 7,480 square meters, the school now has 31 students across three classes, down from about 50 before the nickel factories arrived. Teachers say enrolment has fallen as parents send their children to larger towns and cities to get away from the pollution. Limited funding from the School Operational Assistance (BOS) program means the school cannot hire dedicated cleaning staff, leaving students and teachers to do the sweeping. But no matter how often they clean, the dust returns, along with the constant drone and clang from nearby factories. It was time for the next lesson. Sulfa and her friends ran back to their classroom, passing a wall painted with the words “Child-Friendly School”. The lettering had faded, much like the hopes of Pa’jukukang residents for a better life amid the never-ending dust and drone from nearby nickel smelters. Students at Pa’jukukang State Junior High School (SMPN) 3 play on the school field without masks, even though the school sits beside a nickel smelter complex that sends dust and stench into the air. (Project M/Iqbal Lubis) Note: Project Multatuli has sent requests for comment to Huadi Group by email and via a form on the group’s website, but has not received a response by the time of publication. This photo story, originally published in Indonesian, was translated by Devina Heriyanto. The English-language editor was Viriya Singgih.

title: Journalism in the Age of Prompts: How AI Pushes Newsrooms Deeper into an Existential Struggle for Relevance
